evidenceClaims.claim: Independent biological data points must be distinguished from technical replicates when reporting and interpreting experiments.
evidenceClaims.scope: Preclinical biomedical research and nested experimental measurements.
evidenceClaims.qualification: The independent unit depends on intervention/assignment and sampling structure; patient is not automatically the unit in every design.

evidenceClaims.claim: Randomization and blinding/masking are rigor practices used, when appropriate, to reduce systematic or expectation-related bias.
evidenceClaims.qualification: Not every experiment can be fully randomized or blinded; limitations should be reported.

evidenceClaims.claim: Choosing the appropriate unit of analysis requires understanding technical versus biological replicates.
evidenceClaims.scope: Biomedical experimental design and statistical inference.
evidenceClaims.qualification: The statistical model should reflect the design and dependence structure.
evidenceClaims.supportingLocation: High-priority principles: appropriate unit of analysis

evidenceClaims.claim: Positive and negative controls can establish assay-performance reference points and help distinguish true biological findings from assay failure.
evidenceClaims.qualification: Control choice is assay- and endpoint-specific; not every assay has the same feasible controls.
evidenceClaims.supportingLocation: General concepts in assay development and validation; control samples

evidenceClaims.claim: Weak or absent Western blot signal has multiple plausible technical causes, including inefficient transfer, low target abundance, antibody problems and detection/imaging conditions.
evidenceClaims.qualification: These are candidate causes, not a diagnosis; reagent-specific settings remain system-specific.
evidenceClaims.supportingLocation: General Western blot troubleshooting → Weak or no signal

evidenceClaims.claim: Multiple or diffuse Western blot bands can arise from excessive antibody/protein load, detection conditions or poor antibody specificity; sample degradation can also contribute.
evidenceClaims.qualification: Additional bands may also reflect genuine isoforms or PTMs, so extra bands must not be automatically labeled nonspecific.
evidenceClaims.supportingLocation: Nonspecific or diffuse bands; fluorescent troubleshooting

evidenceClaims.claim: Quantitative Western blotting requires attention to linear range and signal saturation; visually strong bands are not automatically quantitatively reliable.
evidenceClaims.qualification: Linear range depends on antibody, target, detector, exposure and sample amount.
evidenceClaims.supportingLocation: Abstract / strategies for improving Western blot accuracy

evidenceClaims.claim: A housekeeping protein should not be assumed invariant across tissues or treatments without validation; total-protein normalization is a useful alternative in some settings.
evidenceClaims.qualification: Do not teach that total-protein normalization is universally superior.
evidenceClaims.supportingLocation: Abstract: loading-control variability and total-protein alternative

evidenceClaims.claim: Treating technical Western blot replicates as independent biological samples can artificially inflate effective sample size and distort inference.
evidenceClaims.scope: Repeated measurements of the same biological specimens.
evidenceClaims.qualification: Appropriate aggregation or hierarchical modeling depends on design; the blotRig LMM is not a universal default.

evidenceClaims.claim: Antibody validation should be application-specific and can use complementary genetic, orthogonal, independent-antibody or tagged-protein strategies.
evidenceClaims.scope: Antibody-based research including WB and IHC.
evidenceClaims.qualification: No single pillar is universally sufficient for every target/application.

evidenceClaims.claim: Cq values are intermediate qPCR data and should not be treated as fully efficiency-corrected and normalized expression measurements.
evidenceClaims.qualification: Exact quantification depends on assay purpose; MIQE 2.0 recommends efficiency-aware target quantities.
evidenceClaims.supportingLocation: Data Analysis → Target quantity per gene

evidenceClaims.claim: Reference genes used for qPCR normalization require justification and stability assessment because expression may vary with tissue, condition or disease state.
evidenceClaims.qualification: Number and choice of reference genes are context dependent.
evidenceClaims.supportingLocation: Data Analysis → Normalized expression per sample

evidenceClaims.claim: MIQE 2.0 discourages relying on conventional ΔΔCq quantitative analysis because efficiency assumptions, replicate/reference-gene handling and information loss can bias or obscure inference.
evidenceClaims.scope: Quantitative gene-expression qPCR under MIQE 2.0 recommendations.
evidenceClaims.qualification: This is a current guideline recommendation, not a claim that every historical ΔΔCq result is automatically invalid.

evidenceClaims.claim: qPCR control design should distinguish true target signal from technical artifacts; MIQE 2.0 discusses positive, negative, no-template and no-reverse-transcriptase controls.
evidenceClaims.qualification: The applicable control set depends on assay type; no-RT is specific to RT workflows.

evidenceClaims.claim: Amplification in a no-template control can indicate reagent/environmental contamination or cross-contamination and requires investigation.
evidenceClaims.qualification: In intercalating-dye assays, nonspecific products/primer-dimers may also contribute.

evidenceClaims.claim: In SYBR/intercalating-dye qPCR, multiple melt-curve peaks are a specificity warning for multiple products/off-target amplification or primer-dimer and should trigger product-specificity checks.
evidenceClaims.qualification: Melt curves are supportive rather than definitive molecular identification.
evidenceClaims.reviewerNote: Tier C support; leave pending or replace with stronger source.

evidenceClaims.claim: Clinical IHC assays should be analytically validated or verified before patient results are reported.
evidenceClaims.qualification: CAP clinical-laboratory guidance must not be generalized as a regulatory rule for exploratory research IHC.

evidenceClaims.claim: For initial clinical IHC assay validation/verification, CAP 2024 recommends at least 90% overall concordance between the new assay and comparator/expected results.
evidenceClaims.qualification: Do not apply the 90% threshold as a universal rule to exploratory research staining.

evidenceClaims.claim: IHC staining can be materially affected by preanalytical factors such as delay to fixation, fixative type, fixation duration and processing, with antigen-dependent effects.
evidenceClaims.qualification: Do not teach a single universal fixation threshold across all antigens and laboratories.

evidenceClaims.claim: Little or no IHC staining should be interpreted using controls and assay context because the specimen may be truly negative or the staining system may have failed.
evidenceClaims.qualification: Vendor-specific settings are not universal; a validated high-expressing control is one useful discriminator.
evidenceClaims.supportingLocation: Potential Problem: Little to No Staining

evidenceClaims.claim: High IHC background has multiple possible technical sources, including deparaffinization problems, endogenous detection chemistry, secondary cross-reactivity, inadequate blocking or washing.
evidenceClaims.qualification: Which causes apply depends on tissue and detection chemistry.

evidenceClaims.claim: IHC antibody validation should be application-specific and can include expected localization, orthogonal assays, independent antibodies and reproducibility across runs/operators/lots.
evidenceClaims.qualification: The exact validation strategy depends on target biology and intended use.
